heading: Why knowing what to skip could matter more than knowing what to study for the CAT

With the final countdown to the Common Admission Test (CAT) underway, a palpable sense of frenzy often grips aspirants. However, competitive exams like the CAT are less about brute-force intelligence and more about strategic decision-making. The final score is dictated by the number of attempts and accuracy. The secret to turning these two opposing forces into allies lies in mastering a critical skill: strategic skipping.

To understand why skipping is a superpower, first look at the data from past CAT iterations, which reveals that a 99 percentile typically hovers around 50-55% of the total score. Thus, you do not need to attempt half of the paper to secure a 99 percentile. By intentionally relinquishing half the test, you effectively double the time available per attemptable question. However, to pick the correct 50% to solve, you must sharpen your strategy.

The cardinal rule is simple: never miss out on an easy question. When you look at a question, decide immediately whether to attempt it or drop it based on your familiarity with the concept. This ensures that you can navigate to the end of the section within the stipulated time limit. This means:
Attempts go up: Because you are clearing out fast easy wins, you free up time to make multiple passes through the paper, picking up more doable questions in subsequent rounds.

Accuracy goes up: Because you are exclusively engaging with questions within your comfort zone, the probability of making a mistake drops substantially compared to forcing your way through high-difficulty problems.
Knowing how to skip requires different structural approaches depending on the specific section you are tackling.

VARC: Scanning the entire paper first to come back later is inefficient. Most passages and questions require fresh, deep immersion. Read and evaluate the textual clarity or question type immediately, and either solve it right then or leave it behind permanently.

DILR: This section naturally divides itself into distinct blocks or sets. Rather than evaluating individual questions, consider the overarching dataset or logic puzzle. Spend the opening minutes evaluating the sets, select the most approachable ones based on your practice exposure, and skip the highly convoluted sets entirely.

QA: This section features a large volume of independent questions. So, first divide your 40 minutes into 10-minute chunks. Within each 10-minute block, focus strictly on a specific small set of questions. Scan that mini-set for difficulty, solve the easy-to-medium ones immediately, and skip the rest.

Ultimately, question selection is driven by practice and exposure. To back up your ability to skip effectively, your daily preparation must undergo a critical shift in focus: Spend time sharpening core strengths and topics you are already familiar with. Practise diverse variations of known question types to deepen familiarity and allow your mind to immediately recognise a doable question during the actual exam.

Completely avoid the temptation to start brand-new, complex chapters or chase low-yield, obscure concepts out of panic. Trying to study everything at this stage creates mental clutter and dilutes your accuracy. If a topic makes you freeze, learn to accept it as an immediate candidate for skipping rather than a deficit you must fix.
By shifting your focus from what to study to how to execute, you train your mind to refuse difficult questions instinctively.
